newsitem.title: UK: Railtrack rocky ride ahead after bumper year.
newsitem.headline: Railtrack rocky ride ahead after bumper year.

text.p: Railtrack Plc's relentless share price rise since privatisation in May 1996 appears to have run into the buffers as it faces political and regulatory onslaughts from all sides.

The British rail infrastructure giant's sparkling share price performance in recent weeks has lost some of its lustre as it faced criticisms from the new Labour government, its regulator and even some of its customers -- the train operating companies (TOCs) which pay for use of the track, stations and signalling it owns.

One analyst summed up the mood on Tuesday. "The shares have fallen right back in recent weeks. A lot of uncertainty remains and people don't like the idea of some of the ultimatums being given to Railtrack."
Shares have slipped to 615-1/2 pence per share from a high of 697 pence just months ago. That compares with a 410-1/2 pence close after opening trade in 1996.

The most immediate threat looms next week when the new Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown unveils details of his windfall tax on privatised utilities in his first Budget statement.
Some press reports claim Railtrack is in the front of Brown's firing line and could be stung for as much as 500 million pounds ($835.3 million) -- a report which Railtrack denies.
But one transport analyst admitted, "The windfall tax has to be a major risk to the group and investors would be very lucky to escape."
Labour has also sounded a more bearish tone on regulation.

Over the weekend John Prescott, the new Labour government's deputy prime minister and transport head, delivered another blistering warning that Railtrack faced a more hawkish regulatory regime in future.
He told the annual conference of the train drivers' union Aslef that he backed efforts by the Office of the Rail Regulator to beef up its powers to monitor Railtrack's investment commitments.
"I would emphasise that unless a satisfactory arrangement is reached by agreement then the whole question of how Railtrack is regulated will be opened up once more," Prescott said.

In recent weeks, the Rail Regulator John Swift has opened a review into Railtrack's investment performance and is pushing the company to agree to changes to its licence conditions which would give the watchdog greater powers to ensure Railtrack's investment is delivered.
Railtrack has resisted and told Reuters on Tuesday that if no compromise is reached it would push for a referral to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).

"We think we have in place something that works," said Roger Shires, director of public affairs at Railtrack. "We therefore feel we don't need a change to the license... But the MMC would be the last resort."
The next meeting between the two sides is on Thursday, said Railtrack.

A spokesman for the Rail Regulator, told Reuters "We had hoped Railtrack would come along with us on this and agree. But they've said 'No way'. We will now continue talks and try to illicit a response on why they have adopted this stance."

Separate to Railtrack's investment track record, the watchdog is also looking into complaints being made by some of Railtrack customers -- the TOCs -- led by Connex, the south east England rail service operator owned by France's Generale des Eaux.
Connex South Central claims the performance targets for Railtrack in its original franchise agreement was unrealistically low and easy to achieve.
Under the franchise terms, if Railtrack exceeds those targets it receives a payment from the TOC. But if Railtrack falls below the target threshold, Railtrack pays the TOC instead.
"We are in negotiations with Railtrack over the targets. We want to review the benchmark set for the performance regime," a Connex spokesman told Reuters.

Asked whether any other TOCs were also unhappy, he said "I don't think we're alone in this," raising the spectre of Railtrack facing a rash of complaints from the customers which generate the bulk of its revenues.

Railtrack feels these criticisms are unfair. "This performance regime was set up right at the beginning with the TOCs' full agreement. They agreed to the conditions but are now critical because we have done better," said Shires.

Analysts believe that Railtrack has become the new "bete noir" of the privatised utility sector because it has been such a dazzling investment success. Its shares have outperformed even the surging transport sector by 34 percent over the last year or so and by 35 percent when compared to the FT All Share index.
Its first year's pretax profits on June 5 showed bumper 346 million pounds, up 27 percent
"It was bad timing that those results came out when they did," said one industry analyst, attracting attention to Railtrack's profit bonanza just as the criticisms reached a crescendo.
